definition: In computer science and operations research, Fernandez’s bound (FB) is a lower-bounding technique used in exact algorithms for multiprocessor scheduling problems, particularly within branch-and-bound frameworks.
details: It provides tighter lower bounds than some earlier methods (e.g., Hu's bound). Using Big O notation, a naïve computation of the bound requires O(n3) time, as it examines O(n2) task combinations, each taking O(n) time in the worst case. Efficient implementations reduce the complexity to O(n2).

explainer.lead: Fernandez’s bound helps an exact scheduling algorithm estimate how good a multiprocessor schedule could possibly be from a partial solution. A stronger estimate lets branch-and-bound discard more hopeless options without risking the optimal answer.

tiers.eli5: Imagine dividing chores among several people and trying every possible way to assign them. Fernandez’s bound is like a careful estimate saying, “Even in the best case, this plan cannot finish sooner than this time.” If you already have a plan that finishes sooner, you can stop exploring that estimate’s branch.
tiers.practitioner: Evaluate the bound at branch-and-bound nodes for multiprocessor scheduling, then compare it with the best complete schedule found so far. It can provide tighter bounds than Hu’s bound, but it is only a lower bound, not proof that an achievable schedule meets that value. A naïve implementation takes O(n^3) time; efficient implementations reduce this to O(n^2).
tiers.paperLevel: For a scheduling subproblem S with n tasks, let FB(S) denote Fernandez’s lower bound on the optimal value attainable within S; branch-and-bound can discard S when this bound cannot improve on the incumbent. The bound can be tighter than Hu’s bound. Direct evaluation examines O(n^2) task combinations at O(n) worst-case cost each, giving O(n^3), while efficient implementations achieve O(n^2).

explainer.example: Suppose a partial assignment has Fernandez’s bound 18, meaning no completion of that branch can have a value below 18, while Hu’s bound gives only 16. If the search already holds a complete schedule with value 17, the branch can be pruned immediately; with only the weaker bound of 16, that conclusion would not follow.

explainer.goal: Compute a lower bound for a multiprocessor scheduling subproblem so exact search can safely prune branches that cannot beat the best known schedule.
inputs: The tasks in the current scheduling subproblem
Any partial scheduling decisions at the branch-and-bound node
The best complete schedule found so far, for the pruning comparison
outputs: A numerical lower bound for the subproblem
A keep-or-prune decision when compared with the incumbent
steps: Examine the task combinations required by Fernandez’s bound.
Compute the lower bound from those combinations.
Compare the bound with the best complete schedule found so far.
Prune the branch if it cannot improve that schedule; otherwise continue searching.
tradeoffs: Tighter bounds can remove more search branches.
The bound does not itself construct an optimal schedule.
Efficient evaluation reduces the cost to O(n^2).
